submission.natural_language_explanation: Retrospective lexical detector for the vocabulary of quoted, explained and attributed claims: it fires on tokens that name an assertion or its rendering (theory, hypothesis, conjecture, explanation, interpretation, quotation/quote/quoted/excerpt, illustration/Figure, pseudo, rhetoric(al), persuasive, perjury, disinformation, deception, forensic, trivia, curiosity, puzzle) and on the media brands and named people such claims are attributed to (Reuters, BBC, Guardian, Fox News, Twitter, Google, Wikipedia, Dawkins, Rutherford, Aristotle, Van Gogh). It is essentially zero on concrete everyday nouns (window, kitchen, bottle), on generic abstract nouns (value, system, power, process), on academic-process nouns (research, evidence, data, study, results) and on encyclopedic topic words (species, province, century, population); a second, weaker driver raises it on mid-word fragments of foreign words and names (gh, ische, hew, ote, pt), which the claim-vocabulary description does not cover.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The city council met on Tuesday evening to debate the future of the old harbor district, a question that has divided residents for nearly a decade. Supporters of the redevelopment plan argue that new apartments, shops and a riverside walkway would bring jobs and tax revenue to a neighborhood that has struggled since the shipyards closed. Opponents say the plan would displace long-time tenants and destroy the character of the waterfront. The meeting drew a crowd of several hundred people, many of them carrying signs and chanting slogans outside the chamber while the debate continued inside. Police reported no arrests, though tempers ran high during the public comment period. The mayor opened the session with a short statement about the budget, noting that the city had already spent two million dollars on surveys and environmental reviews. Several council members asked whether the money could have been better used on schools and transit. A consultant hired by the city presented a slide show with maps, traffic projections and cost estimates, and answered questions for more than an hour. Most of the discussion focused on parking, flood risk and the fate of a small park where children play after school. Midway through the evening, a resident named Maria Alvarez read a passage from a letter written by her grandmother, who worked in the shipyards during the war. The letter described the noise of the cranes, the smell of salt and oil, and the pride the workers took in their craft. Alvarez then offered a quotation from the city's own 1998 master plan, which promised to preserve public access to the waterfront. 'We are not asking for anything that was not already promised to us,' she said, and the room erupted in applause. A council member asked her to submit the letter and the excerpt from the master plan to the clerk so that both documents could be entered into the record. After the public comment period ended, the council voted seven to four to postpone the final decision until the next meeting, when the planning department is expected to release a revised proposal. The mayor said the delay would give residents more time to read the documents and submit written comments. Outside the chamber, organizers from both sides promised to keep campaigning, and several said they expected an even larger crowd at the next session. The harbor district has been the subject of numerous studies over the years. A 2004 report recommended mixed-use development, and a 2011 survey found that most residents wanted better bus service and more green space. Neither document settled the dispute, and both sides continue to cite them. The planning department is expected to publish a new draft in the spring, followed by a public hearing and another round of comments before the council takes a final vote.
